title: Bea and the Giggle-Snort Spell
markdown:
Gadzooks, but the pond had been a peaceful office until the reeds learned jokes.

Dew lay on the lily pads like a million tiny decisions to sparkle, and the morning air was soft as a secret. It was a weekend morning, the slow kind. Bea the Pond Watcher sat on her favourite mossy stone, eyes the colour of warm earth, watching a fallen leaf make a tiny boat of itself. Beside her leaned Rattle, a friend of dried reeds, his lattice skeleton clattering like gentle rain on a dry roof when the breeze asked him to. They cherished unhurried hours.

Then a rustle began that was not the usual swish of water and wind. It chattered, like tiny wooden teeth with nerves, or a little unkindness. Words spilled that pricked the air.

“Your nose is like a wobbly mushroom,” rasped a reed by the bank.

“And your reflection looks like a grumpy frog,” crackled another, stalks rattling with sudden laughter.

Bea’s eyes widened. Rattle quivered from topmost reed to rooty base. “Whatever is happening to our lovely reeds? They sound ever so cross.”

The pond rippled with more than breeze. Dragonflies darted as if the timetable had changed. On the water the queen swans glided, necks like moonlight, their regal calls gone questioning. Pond folk knew a whispered rule: if peace broke too long, the queens might fly to somewhere calmer. That would be a loss with no good repair.

Bea’s quiet filled with a plan. “Rattle, this isn’t a funny wind. This feels like a spell.”

He rustled the length of himself. “It reminds me of old Willow Whisker by the elderberry, the time he turned tadpoles into tiny giggling pebbles. He said it came from a book of playful forgotten spells.”

A spark of memory: water voles’ hushed tales of a dusty leather book in the Whispering Woods. “The Laughing Spellbook. If our reeds are this unkind, it must be from there.”

A chance boast, as such things go. She had not seen the book. She spoke as if finding it were as simple as naming it. Rattle swayed, willing to be the audience for a trick not yet invented.

They walked toward the ancient trees, swan-calls a soft reminder behind them. The woods were never truly frightening to Bea, only deep: gold shafts, squirrels pausing mid-scurry, field mice peeking from ferns. A path of last year’s leaves made a quiet carpet. Somewhere a woodpecker kept a polite, private rhythm.

“We must find it before the swans decide we are too noisy.”

“Who knows what lives in those pages,” Rattle whispered. “Ladybug hats. Clouds that taste of spun sugar. And, it seems, reeds that tell fibs.”

They tried the obvious tricks first, as a clever tailor tries the seams before the cloth. Bea asked an elder stump if it had seen a book; the stump, being a stump, offered only moss. Rattle leaned into a hollow and listened for laughter that did not belong to birds. A pair of magpies watched, interested in anything that shone, and Bea showed them empty hands. “Not treasure,” she told them. “A nuisance with a cover.” The magpies, unimpressed, took their shine elsewhere.

The air cooled and grew fragrant as the canopy closed. They passed the elderberry where Willow Whisker was said to nap, and Bea left a nod for the tadpole story, just in case stories like to be remembered. Then, in a mossy hollow at the foot of an oak furrowed like a friendly face, they found it: worn cover, lavender and old paper, lying open in a special slant of sun. Nearby woods-reeds kept an expectant hush, as if they, too, had been practising jokes. Golden letters shimmered. A cheerful frog blew a cascade of perfect bubbles.

Bea lifted the book. Aged pages, a little brittle. The rude jokes were not born of malice. A Giggle-Snort Spell had gone too far: the reeds so ticklish with happy energy that unkind words blurted out like sneezes. The book was not wicked. It was overly enthusiastic.

Task one, then: name the mischief. She had done that without a wand.

“It says the spell is a tickle that will not stop. To end it we need the Gentle Hush.” She turned pages. Rattle leaned in with an encouraging click.

There: simpler words in silver ink, peaceful as a held breath. Task two had been the hunt. Task three would be the speaking, a bluff against too much joy, as if hush could out-trick a snort.

She did not slam the book or scold it. That would have been the simple way, and simple ways had already failed the reeds. She read like a lullaby for restless stalks, and she read it twice, because a tickle that will not stop may need to be out-waited as well as out-spoken.

“Hush now, little clatter. Be soft and gentle, like rain on a pane. Let the whispers return, the murmurs of the stream. Peace be upon you, lovely reeds.”

Calm moved from the book through the trees toward the pond. First the woods-reeds by the oak forgot their punchlines. Then, as if a ribbon of quiet had been drawn along the path, the chattering at the water lessened, softened, faded like a dream giving up. Only the familiar swish-swish-swish remained, secrets of water again.

The bank-reeds, which had been rivals in rudeness, now only competed at swaying. One almost began a mushroom-nose remark, heard itself, and turned it into a rustle. That was as close as turning enemies on each other as a pond required.

They closed the book and left it in the hollow, open to the frog page, so the next person would find joy that knew when to stop. Back at the water the queen swans glided with their old serenity, worries thinning like mist. They dipped elegant heads in silent thanks. A real frog, not a drawn one, plopped, which Rattle took as a review.

Bea and Rattle shared a look that did not need a speech. They sat the long way home along the bank, checking each clump: not for perfection, for honesty. Rose and lavender took the sky. The pond became a mirror for the first faint stars.

Rattle settled, barely rustling. Bea did not pile the evening with lessons. She only sat, moss cool through her sleeves, while a last dragonfly wrote a quiet signature on the air. The lily pads kept their diamonds a little longer, then gave them back to the dark.

And if you listen on a still weekend, you may hear a reed almost start a joke, then think better of it. That is the wink: even a Laughing Spellbook can be outfoxed by a girl who reads the next page.
